_min_savings_comment: A listing must clear BOTH discount_threshold_pct (relative) AND min_savings_dollars (absolute) to get flagged. The dollar floor exists to keep trivial deals out, but it was set at $10, which silently excluded the entire cheap end of the hobby: a $4 card worth $12 is 67% off and saves $8, and was being rejected. Lowered to $3, with the anti-junk job moved to cheap_cards below, where it belongs -- being cheap is not the same as being junk, and a dollar floor cannot tell the difference. Ranking in the email is by dollar amount saved, highest first, so cheap finds sort to the bottom naturally and never crowd out real money.

ebay._comment: category_id 212 is eBay's 'Sports Trading Cards' category as of 2026. eBay occasionally renumbers categories -- if active-listing results look wrong, look up the current ID via the Taxonomy API (GET /commerce/taxonomy/v1/category_tree/0) and update this value.

ebay_alerts._comment: Used instead of the eBay API (declined account): reads eBay's own saved-search alert emails from your Gmail account via IMAP. Requires you to first create a saved search + email alert on eBay's site for each watchlist player -- see README 'eBay via saved-search email alerts'. VALIDATED against real alert emails -- see src/ebay_email_alerts.py.
ebay_alerts._mailbox_comment: Searches All Mail, not just Inbox, so you're free to archive alert emails (or filter them straight out of your inbox) without CardPro losing sight of them -- only actually deleting a message (emptying Trash) makes it disappear. Change only if your Gmail account uses a non-English locale where this folder has a different IMAP name.

craigslist._comment: Craigslist blocks automated scraping outright (confirmed against both headless and headed browser automation), so these just build ready-to-click search links included in the daily email instead of being fetched automatically.

valuation._comment: Comp-engine quality gates. These are the difference between a real valuation and a number that just restates the price. min_comps_required: how many comparable observations a bucket needs before it may be used at all. min_distinct_comp_dates / min_comp_span_days: how much CALENDAR SPREAD those observations need. Counting observations alone is not enough -- the daily scan records every listing it sees each morning, so six asks captured in one morning is one snapshot six listings deep, not six independent readings of a market. Hand-entered sold comps are exempt: three real sales on one day are three real transactions. half_life_days: recency weighting -- a comp this many days old counts half as much as one from today. stale_after_days: if the NEWEST comp in a bucket is older than this, the bucket may not declare a deal. max_dispersion: MAD/median above this means the comps disagree too much to trust a median. mad_threshold: outlier trim, in scaled median-absolute-deviations. require_flag_eligible_comp: when true (strongly recommended) only identity-and-grade-matched comp levels may declare a deal -- broader levels are shown as context but can never flag one, which is what stops the circular price-tier comparison that produced every false positive in v1.

economics._comment: Resale assumptions, not facts. Every one of these shows up in the report next to the profit figure so you can see what the number depends on. Tune them to how you actually sell. marketplace_fee_pct 13.25 + $0.30 is eBay's standard trading-card final value fee at time of writing -- verify against your own account. resale_haircut_pct is the gap between the median comp and what you'd realistically get selling it promptly.

auctions._comment: An auction's current bid is not a price. Auctions get their own report section and their own math: max rational bid is the highest you could bid and still keep required_margin_pct of margin against estimated market value, after fees and shipping. ending_soon_hours controls what counts as urgent -- only used for ordering the section, never for relaxing any quality gate.

alerts._comment: Immediate-alert tier. Deliberately conservative: too many alerts destroy the product. An opportunity must clear BOTH of these AND have a flag-eligible comp to earn an out-of-band alert; everything else waits for the morning digest. The dollar figure is 25, not the 150 it was: with focus.price_ceiling at $40 a card cannot save $150 without being worth $190, so a $150 bar meant ACT NOW could never fire on the cards this report is now built around, and an alert tier that cannot fire is not conservative, it is off. Retune this whenever you move focus.price_ceiling -- the two numbers only make sense together.

focus._comment: What reaches the email, and how long it may be. Separate from the deal gate on purpose: the gate decides whether a card is underpriced, this decides whether it is what you shop for. price_ceiling is the cheap end you actually buy and bid at; a dearer card is not called bad, it just has to be exceptional (exceptional_min_discount_pct AND exceptional_min_savings_dollars, off a flag-eligible comp) to take a slot from the cheap ones. Cards on your target list ignore BOTH price rules -- the ceiling and the bidding-room rule -- because you named those cards and set their price yourself, and a target buy_zone normally sits well above the resale-margin ceiling max_rational_bid computes. Never seeing the card you asked for is an invisible failure; a slightly longer email is a visible one. The length cap still applies to targets. require_auction_bidding_room drops auctions already bid past your max rational bid: you cannot win those at a price that works, and they cost the same space as a live one (auctions with no market value have no ceiling to be past, so they stay). max_listings caps the whole email; max_per_section is the first-pass share each section gets before the leftovers are handed out, which is what stops a 40-opportunity morning from printing zero auctions. Nothing dropped here is dropped silently -- the counts and the setting that would bring each group back are printed in the report footer. cool_cards_price_ceiling is a HIGHER ceiling that applies only to cards with something genuinely scarce about them -- a signature or a patch or a serial number -- because "is this the cheap end I shop at" and "is this a card worth looking at" are different questions and a $60 auto fails the first while passing the second. Set enabled=false for the old everything-every-day report.

cheap_cards._comment: Rules that apply only below price_ceiling. Cheap cards need their own gate because 48% of everything CardPro observes is under $10 and most of it is commodity -- base veterans, junk-wax commons, team cards. A 60%-off base common is still a base common. So a cheap card must clear a HIGHER percentage bar (min_discount_pct) and, if require_desirable_attribute is on, must actually have something that makes a copy scarce: rookie, autograph, patch/relic, serial numbering, a non-base parallel, or a grade. Anything cheap with none of those is rejected as common_card and counted in the report footer, not silently dropped. Set enabled=false to apply the ordinary rules at every price.

sold_comps._comment: Hand-entered sold prices -- the only real market data CardPro can get. Every other comp in the system is an ASKING price (a seller's opinion), which is why the engine caps those below 'high' confidence. There is no free, automatable, ToS-respecting sold-price feed: eBay's Marketplace Insights API is closed to new users, Terapeak is manual-only, and scraping breaches terms. So you enter these by hand, usually after looking a card up on 130point.com (free, covers eBay + Goldin, includes accepted Best Offers). A handful of real sales for cards you actually care about is worth more than thousands of asking prices. Add one with: python -m scripts.add_sold_comp --help

report._comment: How the email is organised. cheap_find_ceiling is what counts as pocket change: a card at or under it, with any attribute at all that makes a copy worth having, gets a CHEAP FINDS slot. That section makes no claim that the card is underpriced -- being cheap and being underpriced are different facts and CardPro can establish the first from a title and usually cannot establish the second at all. COOL CARDS is the same idea without the price bound: shown for what the card IS, ordered by how scarce or wanted it is, with no valuation attached. Between them they are the part of the email with something in it on an ordinary day.
